newsitem.title: USA: Stocks rally, bonds little changed before jobs report.
newsitem.headline: Stocks rally, bonds little changed before jobs report.

text.p: Stocks rallied Thursday as Wall Street approached Friday's widely awaited May jobs report with surprising confidence but bonds ended little changed.
The dollar fell against the yen after a key Japanese central bank official raised the prospect of higher Japanese interest rates.
Platinum prices soared. Gold ended higher and oil fell.
The Dow Jones industrial average rose 35.63 points to 7,305.29. In the broader market, advances outpaced declines 1,489 to 957 on volume of 452.6 million on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Nasdaq Composite index rose 10.38 points to 1,390.05.
The broad rally, which first lifted technology stocks but spread quickly to financials, transportation stocks and other sectors, came as a surprise to many on Wall Street.

"It's definitely intriguing the market has the confidence to run up ahead of the employment number," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. "This seems to be a bet on a benign number."
The May employment report is due on Friday. Economists estimate payrolls grew 219,000 during the month.

Stocks got little support from the bond market, where the yield on the benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury was unchanged at 6.88 percent. Also, stock market volume was relatively light, indicating many investors were holding back.
Even so, the session's decidedly upward bias, which saw the Dow rally as many as 80 points, raised eyebrows.
"I certainly wouldn't have guessed today would be the best day of the week," said Marshall Acuff, portfolio strategist at Smith Barney.
One possibility, said Acuff, was that investors had shaken some of the earnings jitters that arose after a flurry of warnings starting last Friday with Intel Corp.
"It looks like the concern this week may really have been about earnings," he said. "Investors may have decided the issues were limited to individual companies."
Technology stocks turned in a particularly solid showing, rebounding after their recent downturn.

The dollar fell to a low of 115.47 Japanese yen, its weakest level vs. the yen in more than a week, but recovered to settle at 115.72 yen late in New York, vs. 116.27 late on Wednesday. The dollar was unchanged at 1.7290 German marks.

Yasuo Matsushita, Governor of the Bank of Japan, told a parliamentary committee that it was important to take pre-emptive policy steps to realise continued growth without inflation. Higher rates in Japan would make Japanese assets more attractive, luring investors into yen-denominated securities and thus boosting the Japanese currency.

Platinum for July delivery at the New York Mercantile Exchange closed up the daily limit of $25 at $436.60 an ounce, a new life-of-contract high. Cash platinum in London was fixed at $440.00, the highest price since Sept. 15, 1995.
July gold rose $2.10 to $344.20 an ounce at New York's Commodity Exchange.
Crude oil fell for a third straight day as growing domestic supply and the prospect of another $2 billion worth of Iraqi oil coming to market weighed on prices.
July crude oil fell 46 cents to $19.66 a barrel at the New York Mercantile Exchange.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 added 19.1 points to 4,576.2. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average shed 123.41 points to 20,488.15.
